ace50751-44b2-507a-97c4-64edc5800962.name: *The Illustrious Men of Budrio*
ace50751-44b2-507a-97c4-64edc5800962.description: These paintings are good examples of the fashion of collecting and cataloguing local memories in a sort of Filopatria (love for one's home-town). This was typical of the baroque age and of the age of the Enlightenment. They are composed of several roundels that had to be filled from time to time with portraits of illustrious citizens. In the first painting are depicted doctors, soldiers, ecclesiastics and venerable men living between the Middle Ages and the Early Counter-reformation. Among them are Mercatello, a medical doctor in Bologna, Antonio Cossa, professor of Law, and Bartolomeo Garganelli, professor of Law and Astronomy. In the second painting, finished in 1799, we find especially ecclesiastics, diplomats and magistrates, philosophers, scientists, medical doctors and theologians: Francesco Muratori, professor of Anatomy, Vincenzo Menghini medical doctor and chemist, the local historian Domenico Golinelli and his son Ludovico, a clergy man; artists such as the follower of the Carracci Giacomo Lippi, the baroque painter Giovanni Battista Caccioli, the set designer Vincenzo Gotti; the architects Alfonso Torreggiani and Giuseppe Tubertini. In the third picture illustrious men not included in the first two are depicted, who were born before the end of the century, like the landscape painter Alberto Melonari, the “quadraturista” Giuseppe Carlo Gotti, the set designer and member of the Bolognese Accademia Clementina Alessandro della Nave, the illustrious chemist and pharmacist, Francesco Maria Coli, professor of the University of Bologna, Domenico Inzaghi and Don Giuseppe Benedetti from whose bequests to the town of Budrio were created the public library and the Pinacoteca.
ace50751-44b2-507a-97c4-64edc5800962.short_description: These paintings, hanging in the first room of the Pinacoteca, celebrate men born in Budrio who became famous in various fields including literature, politics, sciences and arts. Many of them are also part of the history of Bologna and its institutions because, given that they were born in Budrio, they are also Citizens of Bologna.
ace50751-44b2-507a-97c4-64edc5800962.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis; the tradition attributes them to the local painter Faustino Trebbi, for stylistic reasons it is thought he only painted the third one. The other two are probably the work of different artists.
ace50751-44b2-507a-97c4-64edc5800962.obtention: Public Library, then moved to the Pinacoteca (1989).

ad69ad7a-9e01-515e-b676-3ad43b71d387.name: *Portrait of Count Miklós Zichy*
ad69ad7a-9e01-515e-b676-3ad43b71d387.description:
A male portrait set in front of a dark background. The artist has concentrated on the features and characteristics of the sitter, making this a rare example of family portraiture that differs from the traditional type of so-called Ancestors' Galleries.  
In 1740, Count Miklós (Nicolaus) Zichy (1710–1758) became landlord of different possessions in Buda (Budakeszi, Óbuda and Újlak among others). A patron of the arts, he financed the building of churches, public buildings and his own castle, built in 1745, in the centre of Óbuda. The Count became a well known and outstanding personality of the region. This type of portraiture does not make use of the traditional attributes and settings of the so-called Ancestors' Galleries but rather connects Baroque representative portraiture to bourgeois portraits of the early 18th century.
ad69ad7a-9e01-515e-b676-3ad43b71d387.short_description: A Baroque official portrait of Count Miklós (Nicolaus) Zichy (1710–1758), one of the richest landowners of the Buda area and a significant patron of the arts. Zichy financed the building and construction of churches and public buildings and constructed a family palace in Óbuda (Old Buda) in 1745.

af2dcc82-957a-54c2-9a0f-e5e5ba86b4d3.name: Ottoman Clothing Album
af2dcc82-957a-54c2-9a0f-e5e5ba86b4d3.short_description: With the political developments of the 19th century, interest in the East increased steadily in the western world. Everything belonging to the East was the centre of interest for western observers. As a result, close to 160 artists visited Istanbul in the 19th century. Pascal Sébah (1823-86) was a pioneer photographer who worked in Istanbul. Sébah opened a photography studio known as "El Chark " in Pera in 1857. The studio's most successful period started with the Vienna Universal Exhibition in 1873. Sébah formed a partnership with Joaillier Polycarpe in 1885. In 1899, the two partners bought Abdullah Frères's archives. For the Vienna Universal Exhibition in 1873, Pascal Sébah prepared *The Ottoman Clothing Album* to be exhibited at the Ottoman Stand.

b10f4142-3c70-5d92-a683-74544a7543bd.name: *Portrait of Count Sámuel Teleki with Baron Sámuel Brukenthal’s half-length portrait*
b10f4142-3c70-5d92-a683-74544a7543bd.description:
J. M. Stock was a Transylvanian Saxon portrait painter and engraver, who matriculated to the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna in 1763, where he was a pupil of Meytens. From 1771, he studied at the Academy of Engraving in Vienna and afterwards lived in Pozsony (Bratislava). As an art connoisseur in Vienna, he dealt with Sámuel Brukenthal, Governor of Transylvania, and carried out commissions for him. In 1786, the painter gave up his work in Bratislava and went with Brukenthal to Nagyszeben (Sibiu).  
The portrait of Sámuel Teleki with Sámuel Brukenthal in the background is a *Freundschaftsbild* or “friendship picture”. Although they had similar scientific interests, and were both art collectors and founders of a museum and library (Teleki in Marosvásárhely (Târgu Mureş) and Brukenthal in Nagyszeben (Sibiu), the intellectual basis of this “friendship painting” was their freemasonic relationship. Both were members of important lodges in Vienna and helped to initiate and then supervise methodical preparation of an encyclopaedia undertaken by the Masonic Lodge in Nagyszeben (Sibiu); the intention of the project was to cover the history and contemporary conditions of all three nations inhabiting the region.  
Stock portrayed both Teleki and Brukenthal at their desks. Teleki, in Hungarian national costume, poses in a way commonly adopted by scientists and is within a context suggestive of a study. In the background, Brukenthal is portrayed dressed in casual garments in the pose of a French encyclopaedist-philosopher; the portrait provides a fitting detail for the interior. In addition, the picture includes motifs relating to freemasonry for on the desk, among other objects suggesting scientific study, is a map of Háromszék county in Transylvania showing the names of cities particularly active in freemasonry. The bust of Joseph II, also on the desk, is significant in that the Edict of Tolerance issued by the Emperor in 1781, made Sámuel Teleki's public career possible permitting, amongst other things, his appointment as Vice Chancellor of Transylvania in 1787.
b10f4142-3c70-5d92-a683-74544a7543bd.short_description: Johann Martin Stock was a well-educated portrait painter and graphic artist in Nagyszeben (Sibiu) and Pozsony (Bratislava). This portrait is a *Freundschaftsbild* or “friendship picture” of the library's founders, the Transylvanian count Sámuel Teleki and his friend, Baron Sámuel Brukenthal, whose portrait is in the background.
b10f4142-3c70-5d92-a683-74544a7543bd.method_for_datation: The painting, both signed and dated, portrays two men whose identities have been confirmed with the help of engravings.
b10f4142-3c70-5d92-a683-74544a7543bd.obtention: Transferred from the City Art Gallery to the Museum of Fine Arts where it was up until 1974, when it was moved to the Hungarian National Gallery.

b1761f2e-80b8-586f-b4e2-c3736d979725.name: Photograph of an employee outside the *Poste-Cherifienne* office
b1761f2e-80b8-586f-b4e2-c3736d979725.description: The first national post and transport service in Morocco was founded by Mulay al-Hasan I on 20 Jumada I 1390 (22 November 1892) and was known as the *Poste-Makhzen*. The office was established in order to take control nationally of the postal (mainly parcels and messengers) service in Morocco, but competition from private foreign firms was tough. When in 1892 the Sultan first gave orders for port managers to take control of Morocco’s interests in this regard, this nascent organisation included 13 Moroccan cities, defined as zones connected by transport links, and each defined by specific costs.

b2f01795-06d0-53f5-977b-6664d2f2de6b.name: *King João V of Portugal Drinking Coffee and Chocolate*
b2f01795-06d0-53f5-977b-6664d2f2de6b.description:
This interesting miniature, set within an ornate silver frame displaying the royal coat of arms, is one of only a few remaining objects from the Joanine court to have survived the Earthquake of 1755. According to the family of the Marquis of Foz, to whose collection this miniature belonged until 1901, this scene represents King João V being served drinking chocolate at home by the Duke of Lafões. However, in the corner of the miniature is the date 1720, making the Foz identification of the duke implausible given that the duke was born in 1718 and would have been two years old at the time this picture was painted. The most plausible hypothesis is that the person depicted is Prince Miguel of Braganza, the half-brother of the King and father of the future Duke of Lafões, who would, therefore, be the child represented. The Foz family also asserted that the Marquises of Angeja and Alegrete appear in the painting, as well as the painter himself and the house chaplain, however, firm identifications have been neither consistently contradicted nor confirmed.  
The objects depicted in this composition are noteworthy: the utensils associated with painting are in the foreground: a pallet, brushes and a sketch on a piece of paper. The objects related to drinking: a coffee pot, hot chocolate maker, tea cups and a bottle, alluding to the popularity of chocolate and coffee both of which became extremely fashionable among the Portuguese aristocracy and throughout the rest of Europe.  
Although the scene suggests a relaxed and jolly atmosphere, the strict etiquette and hierarchy of the Joanine court is present within the structure of the composition: the representational field is divided into two halves, with the higher ranking figures on the left-hand side.  
Nothing is known about the identity of the miniaturist, although his name suggests that he might be one of many Italian artists who, together with other foreigners, came to work in Portugal during the reign of João V. The frame presents plant-like decorations with acanthus, volutes and shell shapes in chiselled and embossed silver – a feature associated with the first quarter of the 1700s. The frame is surmounted by a shield and crowned with the Portuguese royal arms sustained by two lieutenant *putti.* A grotesque mask at the bottom centre is typical of this phase of the Baroque period. A chiselled frieze with laurel leaves serves as an internal frame for the miniature.

b38891de-f49d-5dd2-b4f0-dec5aad2f1bf.name: Carpet-Qajar Portrait
b38891de-f49d-5dd2-b4f0-dec5aad2f1bf.short_description:
This wool rug depicts fifty-one prominent personalities across history in an assemblage portrait. Like many Iranian carpets in the 19th century, this textile reflects the emergence during the Qajar dynasty of pictorial carpets displaying religious, historical or literary scenes.  
Among prophets like Moses, Solomon, and Jesus, are men known throughout Asian history such as Genghis Khan and Confucius. In addition, Socrates, Christopher Columbus and Napoleon Bonaparte contribute to this group portrait.  
  
The border, an essential element in Persian carpets, frames the scene of famous people with floral patterns and a legend with the names of individuals. Interestingly, the numbers appear mirrored, suggesting that the carpet maker was illiterate or unfamiliar with Arabic numbers, leaving his mark within the thread.

b5774f3e-8016-55ca-9542-099e3ef271b9.name: Portrait of Akbar in old age
b5774f3e-8016-55ca-9542-099e3ef271b9.short_description: This posthumous portrait of the Mughal emperor Akbar (r. 1556-1605 CE) was probably commissioned by his grandson Shah Jahan (r. 1628-58 CE), who was thirteen when the emperor died. The aged Akbar is depicted in three-quarter profile, a view reserved for figures of lesser rank but perhaps accepted for posthumous emperor portraits. Mughal conventions such as the golden halo and the fact that the emperor stands upon the orb of the world signify Akbar’s power as a ruler. The intricate details of his embroidered robe and sash, the pearls around his neck, and the bejewelled dagger hilt emphasize his royal standing and are complemented by a scrolling vegetal border rendered in gold. On the border of the album page, believed to be contemporary with the portrait, three of the emperor’s attendants stand symbolically (and literally) behind him, respectively holding his umbrella, standard, and shield. Two puttis, winged angelic figures derived from European models, hold a golden canopy protectively over Akbar’s portrait, while the antelope and deer depicted below, also on the earthly orb, associate the reign of the late emperor with a peaceful era. This portrait is believed to come from Shah Jahan’s last album, the compilation of which began around 1650 CE, and may never have been completed. Its paintings include several single-figure portraits that acted as models for future albums (Canby 1998, p. 151). The numerous border paintings are extremely developed and skilful works of art in their own right. In the early twentieth century, the “Late Shah Jahan Album” was unfortunately dispersed, and the pages, often split into two, were sold separately.

b70d09b4-b304-5766-96c2-44d09249f330.name: *Portrait of Carlo Broschi called Farinelli*
b70d09b4-b304-5766-96c2-44d09249f330.description: This painting is a portrait of the world famous soprano castrate singer Carlo Broschi whose stage name was Farinelli. He is wearing a cape of the order of Calatrava as in 1750 he was made a Knight of this important Spanish order by the king of Spain Ferdinand VI. The singer touches a page of music laid on the cembalo with his left hand. In the background, oval portraits of the King of Spain and his queen, Maria Barbara di Braganza, are surrounded by a tripudium of nymphs and cupids. There is also a self-portrait of the painter, Corrado Giaquinto. The portrait was part of Farinelli’s rich collection of paintings decorating his villa in Bologna, where he retired after a long stay at the court of Madrid (1737–1759).

b76ae0c2-5d4f-563b-9c84-b8b5747b1e2f.name: Ivan V Drašković (about 1660–Varaždin, Croatia, 4.1.1733)
b76ae0c2-5d4f-563b-9c84-b8b5747b1e2f.description:
For generations the Drašković family played an important part in the political and social life of Croatia. Counts from the 17th century (1631), numerous members of the family became *bans* (viceroys) and high-ranking military officers. The family's wealth comprised numerous estates, among which were Trakošćan and Klenovnik castles in northwest Croatia. Ivan V Drašković, son of vice-marshal Ivan IV and Marija Magdalena Nádasdy, studied in Varaždin, Vienna and Bologna before returning to Croatia in 1695. In 1699, he became Grand Sheriff of the Valpovo and Baranja County, and shortly after became a royal councillor. Having excelled militarily, promotion to General followed in 1708 and the Croatian parliament named him Commander of the Croatian National Troops. He actively supported the proposal to ensure the right of succession of the Habsburg female line (Croatian Pragmatic Sanction) in 1712. He fought as vice-marshal (*podmaršal*) on the Turkish border. Drašković was acting *ban* (viceroy) from 1718 to 1732 but only officially appointed to the post on 2 February 1732. He died suddenly the following year.  
The portrait, painted some time shortly after Drašković officially became *ban* in 1732, depicts the elderly count as a nobleman, his right hand holding a general's baton. On the right-hand side, the imperial eagle holds the coats of arms of Croatia, Slavonia and Dalmatia, signifying his official status as *ban*. In the background to the left is Trakošćan castle, with tents and soldiers below.
b76ae0c2-5d4f-563b-9c84-b8b5747b1e2f.short_description: Count Ivan V Drašković was acting *ban* (viceroy) from 1718 to 1732. Officially appointed *ban* on 2 February 1732, he died suddenly the following year. Drašković actively supported the right of succession to the Habsurg female line (Croatian Pragmatic Sanction). The portrait, painted some time shortly after Drašković officially became *ban*, depicts the elderly count as a nobleman, his right hand holding a general's baton.
b76ae0c2-5d4f-563b-9c84-b8b5747b1e2f.initial_owner: The Kulmer family, Šestine near Zagreb
b76ae0c2-5d4f-563b-9c84-b8b5747b1e2f.method_for_datation: The imperial eagle holding the coats of arms of Croatia, Slavonia and Dalmatia signifies the office of *ban* (viceroy), and enables the painting to be conclusively dated to 1732 or 1733.
b76ae0c2-5d4f-563b-9c84-b8b5747b1e2f.obtention: Donated to the Museum by Countess Josipa Kulmer from Šestine near Zagreb in 1854.

b7e5dd09-cf9b-5310-9343-8db43d0c9114.name: *The Emperor of Austria ascending the Great Pyramid*
b7e5dd09-cf9b-5310-9343-8db43d0c9114.short_description: William Simpson wrote in his autobiography: "I went out one day and saw the Emperor of Austria lugged to the top of the Great Pyramid by two Arabs as if he had been only an overland passenger". Many visitors were unceremoniously hauled to the top of the monument by local inhabitants, helping unfit and often overweight tourists to clamber up the huge blocks. Emperor Franz Joseph was one of many European dignitaries in Egypt in November 1869 for the opening of the Suez Canal. Simpson was employed by the Illustrated London News as their "Special Artist". Photography would soon replace such drawings.
keywords: Suez

bc4ebe5a-094c-56c1-b426-f1d720ea5206.name: Abdülaziz (1830–1876)
bc4ebe5a-094c-56c1-b426-f1d720ea5206.short_description: Portrait of Abdülaziz (1830–1876). In 1861 he became Sultan. He was very interested in fostering a good relationship with European powers and to this end visited Paris, London and Vienna in 1867. Because of the uprisings in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Bulgaria, he was forced to abdicate on 30 May 1876.
keywords: Abdülaziz; Bosnia-Herzogivna; Bulgaria; Vienna

bcbffbcf-b106-5603-ac6b-c0832f43b411.name: *Josip Kazimir Drašković* (4.3.1716 – Klenovnik, Croatia, 9.10.1765)
bcbffbcf-b106-5603-ac6b-c0832f43b411.description:
The Drašković family played an important role in the political and social life of Croatia throughout many generations. Counts from the 17th century (1631), numerous members of the family were Croatian *bans* (viceroys) and high-ranking military officers. The family's wealth included numerous estates, among them Trakošćan and Klenovnik castles in northwest Croatia. Josip Kazimir Drašković, son of viceroy Ivan V, was a prominent high-ranking officer, a colonel by the age of 30, and a general by 1750. He took part in quenching the peasants' and soldiers' uprising in Croatia in 1755. In 1758, Empress Maria Theresia awarded him her Military Order for outstanding bravery in the defence of Olomouc; in 1765, he was awarded the Commander's Cross of the same Order for defending Moravia. He was married to Suzana Malatinski with whom he had three sons and a daughter.  
The portrait, originally in Trakošćan, was probably part of the Gallery of Officers serving under Josip Kazimir, consisting of 50 portraits (the other portraits are in Trakošćan Castle Museum). The portrait is the work of the Viennese painter, Johann Michael Millitz. Between 1764 and 1778, he painted numerous members of the Croatian and Hungarian nobility, and painted Josip Kazimir's daughter Julijana (married to Count Erdödy). Drašković is shown wearing a Commander's Cross of Maria Theresia's Military Order. The portrait, modified probably in 1765, commemorates the higher order of Commander's Cross, over-painting the Military Order received by Drašković in 1758.
bcbffbcf-b106-5603-ac6b-c0832f43b411.short_description: Count Josip Kazimir Drašković, son of viceroy Ivan V, was a prominent high-ranking officer promoted to general in 1750. He took part in quenching the peasants’ and soldiers’ uprising in Croatia in 1755. In 1758, Empress Maria Theresia awarded him the Military Order, and in 1765, he was awarded the Commander’s Cross of the same Order.
bcbffbcf-b106-5603-ac6b-c0832f43b411.method_for_datation: The date and origin of the portrait were established through information known about Josip Kazimir Drašković as well as by stylistic analysis of the painting and other known works by Johann Michael Millitz.

bcbffbcf-b106-5603-ac6b-c0832f43b411.obtention: Received from the Commission for the Collection and Preservation of Cultural Monuments and Antiques in 1952.

bcebbe38-8019-5c28-b4b7-8f04a8b1d7be.name: Ibrahim Pasha (1789–1848)
bcebbe38-8019-5c28-b4b7-8f04a8b1d7be.short_description: Portrait of Ibrahim Pasha (1789–1848). As the best General under his father Muhammad 'Ali Pasha, he fought successfully against the Wahhabites, the Ottoman Army and the Greeks. In 1831 he conquered Syria and governed it until 1841. In 1848 he deposed his senile father and was declared Vice King of Egypt by Sultan Abdülmecid I.
keywords: Ibrahim Pasha; Syria; Greece

be995e66-cbb2-5c08-8546-d64d8f9a6fa0.name: Cameo
be995e66-cbb2-5c08-8546-d64d8f9a6fa0.short_description: This oval shaped cameo depicts the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan (r. AH 1037-1068 / AD 1628-1658). He is shown in profile, richly jewelled, a model most likely taken from Mughal paintings. A small group of securely dated cameos exist from the period of Shah Jahan, all of which have been attributed to European lapidaries who worked at the court of the emperor. Cameos like this one continued to be made in later centuries, often by Indian lapidaries, and set into jewelled pendants to be worn.

bf3df40c-9dbc-5641-863e-11c7fa684ee3.name: *Mature Self-portrait*
bf3df40c-9dbc-5641-863e-11c7fa684ee3.description:
The exact date of the self-portrait is unknown, but the slightly greying temples suggest that the artist was about forty. This hypothesis is consistent with the style of the period, which many scholars have likened to the emotional sensitivity of his contemporary, Velázquez.  
Bernini painted only for himself, creating portraits, and in particular self-portraits, in private. He did not seek physiognomic detail or self-aggrandisement, focusing instead on researching psychology and the reality of the human condition. These features give painting back that immediacy which makes his paintings a precursor of the modern Borghese portrait.  
The brush strokes are fast and spontaneous, the shaking effects helping to humanise the subject. The background of the painting appears not to be finished, concentrating our attention on the expression of the face, whose features are rendered by deep chiaroscuro and colouring attributable to Annibale Carracci.  
The head is turned slightly away from the profiled bust. This arrangement suggests a slight movement of the face toward the viewer, accentuated by subtle movement of the hair caused by the twisting.  
Bernini uses strong combinations of light and shadow to add intensity to the eyes, which are almost sculptural in form.  
No documentation has ever been found to confirm the hypothesis that this canvas was taken from a diptych, whose pendant was the portrait of Costanza Bonarelli, the woman Bernini loved. The right-hand side of the canvas is frayed, hence the assumption that this is indeed part of that split work.  
The painting was donated to the Galleria Borghese in 1911 by Baron Otto Messinger, who owned a substantial body of works from the Chigi collection. It is, therefore, assumed that this famous self portrait came from the same place.
bf3df40c-9dbc-5641-863e-11c7fa684ee3.short_description:
This painting demonstrates the self-awareness of the artist, whose pose betrays his preoccupation with intellectual discovery.  
Bernini created many self-portraits during his career.

bf8c236d-a3f0-57db-aaff-72a234666a2c.name: Portrait of Sultan Selim II
bf8c236d-a3f0-57db-aaff-72a234666a2c.short_description: This large album portrait of Sultan Selim II (reigned 1566–74) reveals much about his reign. It was Selim’s father, Sultan Süleyman the Magnificent (reigned 1520–66), who solidified the geographical borders of the Ottoman Empire and refined the central administration of his government, allowing his son and successor to pursue more sedentary pleasures such as literature, art and wine-drinking. Nicknamed “Selim the Sot” for his affection for wine, the sultan was nonetheless a great bibliophile and patron of architecture, music and the arts of the book. The painter, poet and naval commander Haydar Reis depicted Selim II as larger than life; the robust sultan in his luxurious fur-lined and brocaded gold garment dwarfs both the page boy and the interior in which he sits in a cross-legged position on a carpet. This composition was one of a number of conventions for Ottoman royal portraiture developed in the 1570s and is similar to portraits in Loqman’s *Kiyafetu’l Insaniye fi Semailu’l-Osmaniye*, a study to record the physiognomy of the Ottoman sultans.
bf8c236d-a3f0-57db-aaff-72a234666a2c.obtention: Former Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan Collection
keywords: Folio; work-on-paper; works-on-paper; painting; portrait; sultan; ruler

bf8ccf55-0b9f-51ab-833d-046d658d52ad.name: *Mahmud II, Sultan of Turkey* (1784–1839)
bf8ccf55-0b9f-51ab-833d-046d658d52ad.short_description:
Portrait of Mahmud II, Sultan of Turkey (1784–1839). In 1826 Mahmud II initiated the development of a modern army. This led to the uprising of the Janissary, which was quelled by massacring the rebellious troops. Under Mahmud II's reign, in 1821 the Greeks started their fight for freedom which was granted to them in the Peace of Adrianople in 1829.  
After the destruction of the Janissary, the Ottoman Empire under Sultan Mahmud II had only 35,000 badly trained regular soldiers in 1827. Due to the weakness of the Ottoman Empire, Ibrahim Pasha, the son of Muhammad 'Ali (ruler of Egypt), invaded Syria. On 20 February 1832, the Egyptian Army defeated the Ottoman Army at the Battle of Konya. This forced Mahmud II to sign the Peace of Kütahya and to cede Syria and Kilikia to Egypt.
keywords: Mahmud II, Sultan of Turkey; Egypt; Janissary; Konya; Ibrahim Pasha; Muhammad Ali; Greece

c16fad3d-de00-51aa-b32f-c08f9761a3dc.name: *Madame X*
c16fad3d-de00-51aa-b32f-c08f9761a3dc.short_description: The basis of Turkish painting drawing influence from western tradition was laid when *Mühendishane-i Berr-i Hümayun* (the Naval Academy) opened in 1795. Halil Pasha was foremost among the painters with a military background who founded a western-style art tradition in Turkey. He worked with Jean Leon Gerome in his atelier in Paris. He provided a unique distinction to the analysis of impressionist light and colour, and was an example of artists dealing with impressionist technique. Because of his qualified knowledge about anatomy and his interest in depicting the human figure, Halil Pasha had a unique place in Turkish Art History.
keywords: Painting; Halil Pasha; orientalist Turkish painters

c2b70678-bfae-5de0-a210-547e266d7099.name: Emigrant family
c2b70678-bfae-5de0-a210-547e266d7099.short_description: The 1923 population exchange between Greece and Turkey was based upon religious identity, and involved the Greek Orthodox citizens of Turkey and the Muslim citizens of Greece. The "Convention Concerning the Exchange of Greek and Turkish Populations" was signed at Lausanne, Switzerland, on 30 January 1923, by the governments of Greece and Turkey. This photograph belongs to the Luka Likidis family, who migrated from Bodrum to Crete in 1916.
c2b70678-bfae-5de0-a210-547e266d7099.holder: Population Exchange Museum (The Foundation of Lausanne Treaty Emigrants)
keywords: migration; population exchange

c41a0993-462a-5165-a2e7-78834dccf500.name: *Bust of Cardinal Domenico Ginnasi*
c41a0993-462a-5165-a2e7-78834dccf500.description:
In 1911 the bust was found in the Carmelite Convent at the Church of Santa Maria della Vittoria, relocated from the Church of SS. Pietro e Marcellino, the seat of the Teresian Nuns. The nuns moved there in 1757, from the convent founded after the death of Domenico Ginnasi in Palazzo Ginnasi in 1639, and they took the bust with them, having always identified it as a portrait of the cardinal.  
The work was first attributed to both Bernini and Algardi, before being linked to Giuliano Finelli following comparison with the bust the sculptor made for the cardinal for his funeral monument at S. Lucia dei Ginnasi (the decoration is based on a design by Lanfranco, whose daughter married Finelli).  
The sculptor worked with Bernini on several occasions, notably on *Apollo and Daphne* in the Galleria Borghese and the baldachin (large sculpted bronze canopy over the altar) of Saint Peter's. He worked alone from 1629 and joined Rome's artistic circle thanks to the numerous contacts that he was able to make, notably Pietro da Cortona, who in turn introduced him to the Sacchetti family, well known patrons.  
His style is characterised by attention to detail, intense skill and psychological depth, but always retaining spontaneity and immediacy, a peculiarity of Bernini's so-called “talking portrait”. The partially unbuttoned *mozzetta* (a short elbow length cape worn by Catholic clergy), the kindly and informal face and the realistic lines are clear evidence of this style.  
In relation to this, a *Bust of Cardinal Scipione Borghese* made by Finelli and currently in the Metropolitan Museum of New York, was sculpted at the same time as the Bernini version (1632). In 1634 Finelli moved to Naples, where he developed a portrait style closer to Parthenopean and Spanish taste, preferring distant, official, commemorative portraits. However in the work undertaken at this time for Roman clients, he never completely abandoned his refined virtuosity and keen psychological study, as can be seen in the bust of Cardinal Ginnasi, sculpted in 1639.
c41a0993-462a-5165-a2e7-78834dccf500.short_description: A pupil of Bernini, Finelli focused his attention on the particular rather than the whole. This tendency prevented Finelli from being a great statuary artist, although it enabled him to evolve a striking flair for portraiture.
c41a0993-462a-5165-a2e7-78834dccf500.provenance: Carmelite Convent in Santa Maria della Vittoria
c41a0993-462a-5165-a2e7-78834dccf500.obtention: Carmelite Convent in Santa Maria della Vittoria, 1911.

c4f3ee34-3e55-5cf6-ab02-eee9f50cdc11.name: *Danilo I, Prince of Montenegro (1871–1939)*
c4f3ee34-3e55-5cf6-ab02-eee9f50cdc11.short_description: Danilo I, Prince of Montenegro (1871–1939) as a child. Danilo was the eldest son of King Nicola I of Montenegro. He was married to Princess Jutta von Mecklenburg-Strelitz and had to leave Montenegro after it was integrated in the kingdom of Yugoslavia after WWI. He died in 1937 in Vienna, Austria – in exile.

c7278b24-cf58-5191-9342-586e5560d4ff.name: *Mlle. Lauta, first* \[French\] *woman to get a degree in philosophy*
c7278b24-cf58-5191-9342-586e5560d4ff.short_description: Léontine Zanta (not Lauta, as indicated by the photograph) was the first French woman to receive a literature degree (not a philosophy degree), writing her thesis on revival of Stoicism in the 16th century. A journalist, teacher and novelist, she was also very interested in feminism.

c783fc3a-6b1b-58c1-83a4-ba0e00d74936.name: A teacher and one of his pupils
c783fc3a-6b1b-58c1-83a4-ba0e00d74936.short_description: Pictured here are schoolteacher teaching his young pupil to write.

c7f58b8f-d101-5a99-a3cc-dcb898bbfeeb.name: An Algerian woman grinds her meal in an old wooden mill
c7f58b8f-d101-5a99-a3cc-dcb898bbfeeb.short_description: Many Western photographers took great interest in women's daily lives, or in daily rural tasks. In this photograph from 1920 an Algerian woman is pictured as she grinds wheat with a wooden pestle and mortar.

c95dc265-e63b-5039-8f8f-a2652ee2dcba.name: Tripolitania (Libya). Italian soldiers in front of a Roman mosaic
c95dc265-e63b-5039-8f8f-a2652ee2dcba.short_description:
Italian soldiers in front of a Roman mosaic in Tripolitania, Libya. At their feet, almost at the centre of the photo, a plaque explains that: “These wonderful remains of Ancient Rome art and civilization” have been brought back to the admiration of posterity by the Italian soldiers of the Bersaglieri 33rd Battalion in 1911 and they “confirm… Italy’s right to rule over Tripolitania”.  
The plaque explicitly claims that Italy colonial ambitions over Libya were legitimate because Ancient Rome had once ruled over that territory. This line of argument was often used by Italian colonialists in order to legitimize Italian colonial ambitions over Libya.
c95dc265-e63b-5039-8f8f-a2652ee2dcba.holder: Central Institute for Cataloguing and Documentation (ICCD)
c95dc265-e63b-5039-8f8f-a2652ee2dcba.author: Giulia Barrera

c9c74f64-866f-5104-9cb6-e6c2fc0927e4.name: *O Grupo do Leão*
c9c74f64-866f-5104-9cb6-e6c2fc0927e4.short_description: This is a Portuguese new generation of artists who played a major role in naturalist and realist painting in Portugal. Meant to decorate the beer house, this painting became famous and marked the beginning of a period of great artistic activity. This painting by Columbano Bordalo Pinheiro (1857–1929), the greatest painter of his time, depicts a group of artists who got together at the “Leão de Ouro” beer house in Lisbon.

c9d97b65-0be6-5a7c-984a-641093ced2e4.name: *Portrait of Count Maxmilián Oldřich Kounic*
c9d97b65-0be6-5a7c-984a-641093ced2e4.description:
This rendition of a young count in informal brocade clothes and a lace housecoat stands out from the routine official court portraits of its time by virtue of its soft rendering in relaxed brush strokes. The spontaneity and lightness of the work correspond with the personality of a youth known to be devoted to “aristocratic” pastimes such as dancing, horse riding, fencing and playing the guitar. The young count travelled twice to the court in Düsseldorf to get to know his future wife, heiress of the Rietberg County. Maxmilián Oldřich Kounic (1679–1746), later the Moravian provincial governor, undertook the grand tour in 1698, visiting The Hague, Brussels and finally Paris, where he had his portrait painted by a Flemish artist who moved through the elegant Roman and Paris milieu.  
The Kounic family was among the most powerful in Moravia. Maxmilián Oldřich's father, Dominik Ondřej Kounic, was the imperial vice-chancellor, his son Václav Antonín Dominik (1711–1794) became a leading diplomat, court and state chancellor under the reign of four emperors, Maria Theresa, Joseph II, Leopold II and Francis II. Václav Antonín Dominik also promoted the ideas of the Enlightenment; he established the Academy of Science and *Belle Lettres* in Brussels and united the Vienna Academy. Maxmilián Oldřich Kounic was responsible for selecting painters to decorate the Assembly Hall of the Provincial Estates in Brno, and played an important part in the reconstruction of the Kounic family residence in Slavkov, the design of which was among the first examples of the French chateau plan in Moravia.
c9d97b65-0be6-5a7c-984a-641093ced2e4.short_description: This rendition of a young count stands out from the routine official court portraits of its time by virtue of its soft rendering in relaxed brush strokes. The portrait came into existence during the grand tour of Maxmilián Oldřich Kounic, who later became the Moravian provincial governor.
c9d97b65-0be6-5a7c-984a-641093ced2e4.method_for_datation: Letters that survive from Count Kounic’s grand tour elucidate the circumstances of the portrait’s origin. Dominik Ondřej Kounic wanted to commission a portrait of his son the size of which was to be identical to that of his own portrait by Hyacinth Rigaud. His son wanted to know whether to choose Rigaud or Gottfried Kneller to portray him, and asked his father to send him the dimensions of the picture marked by knots on a string as he believed nobody in France would understand Moravian measurements. Unfortunately, the count’s choice of portrait artist is not covered by further correspondence. Marie Mžyková has suggested, on the basis of a style analysis backed by the comparison of X-rays, that the artist was Jakob Ferdinand Voet, a court portraitist from Antwerp.
c9d97b65-0be6-5a7c-984a-641093ced2e4.obtention: The painting was part of the Kounic collection in Slavkov Chateau, near Brno. It is currently administered by the Institute of National Heritage, Brno.

cff9d211-aedd-5f72-abe6-63319cd03d80.name: Photograph of Krste Petkov Misirkov
cff9d211-aedd-5f72-abe6-63319cd03d80.short_description: Krste Misirkov (1874–1926) was a grandiose and profoundly nationally designated personage of the 19th century. He lived in St. Petersburg and was an esteemed and highly engaged member of the Slav-Macedonian Scientific Literary Society. He contributed to the standardization of the modern Macedonian language, having given responses to some important issues of the history, culture and language of Macedonians.

d12751a5-ab84-5160-b99b-ce28227573a2.name: The embroiderers of Dar al-Kiswa in Cairo
d12751a5-ab84-5160-b99b-ce28227573a2.short_description:
Dar al-Kiswa started life as *warshat al-kharanfash* – a large factory established by Muhammad ‘Ali Pasha in 1817 in Cairo. 4000 young men from Cairo were assembled to work there as apprentices in a variety of crafts and trades. But by the 1880s, it had become a workshop dedicated to the production of the Meccan textiles. The workshop was closed down in the late 1990s.  
  
At its heyday, up to a hundred weavers, artisans and embroiderers were known to have worked in Dar al-Kiswa. One section of the workshop, the *qism al-zarkasha*, was responsible for embroidering the textiles that were sent to Mecca every year. Many were members of the same family and often started work there as young boys, remaining until they retired. In the 1930s thre were at least 60 there, with an average age of about 65.  
  
The photographs are of some of the employees working in the embroidery section at Dar al-Kiswa. It is not known when they were assembled, but it is likely to have been sometime around the 1940s–early 50s.

d1d2c280-9bfc-5ff6-9d5a-7ba47f268569.name: *An Aristocratic Couple as Adam and Eve*
d1d2c280-9bfc-5ff6-9d5a-7ba47f268569.description:
*An Aristocratic Couple as Adam and Eve* is a very unusual, bizarre picture of the genre; an allegorical portrait that allowed the artist to ignore the formalities of traditional portraiture. The couple, wearing white wigs and sitting in the garden of Eden among tame wild animals obviously commissioned the painting, but their identities are still unknown. Because of the boldness of the portrayal it is very likely that the painting was the result of an established friendship between the artist and the commissioner, particularly as this kind of portrayal is unparalleled in Millitz's oeuvre as he painted mainly traditional, representative half-length portraits.  
As we know little about Millitz's genre or group portraits and still less about his portraits with landscape elements, this allegorical portrait implies an unusual and new venture for the painter. The basis for the faces was probably traditional portraiture, but for the other parts of the composition the painter in all likelihood used a French sample picture, perhaps suggested by his commissioner. A composition of Adam and Eve by Jean Francois Troy (1679–1752) painted in 1730 is a case in point. This work shows the moment of the Fall of Adam and Eve in a style similar to the Rococo genre but with real emotion. Regards the content of this painting, it portrays the travesty of the biblical scene from the perspective of the Age of Enlightenment. As to its philosophical background, the scene is an enlightened transformation of the free will of the first human couple who acted independently of God's wish.  
Millitz was Martin van Meytens' pupil at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna. He lived and worked in Vienna from 1749 and then worked in Pozsony (Bratislava) between 1778 and 1784. He executed several commissions for mainly Hungarian aristocratic families.
d1d2c280-9bfc-5ff6-9d5a-7ba47f268569.short_description: An unusual representation by the master of Pozsony (Bratislava) painted while Millitz was studying in Vienna: the double nude composition was born under the influence of the new philosophical ideas of the Age of Enlightenment.

d1d8cb50-1251-5dab-a6ce-97b1c120592b.name: Petar Zrinski  (Vrbovec, Croatia, 6.6.1621–Wiener Neustadt, 30.4.1671)
d1d8cb50-1251-5dab-a6ce-97b1c120592b.description:
A descendant of a noble and distinguished Croatian family, Count Petar Zrinski excelled in battles against the Turks. After the death of his elder brother Nikola (d. 1664) – Croatian *ban* (viceroy) and a most prominent Hungarian poet of his time – Petar became *ban* from 1665 to 1671. He translated – from Hungarian to Croatian – Nikola's poem *Adrianskoga mora Syrena* (The Siren of the Adriatic Sea). He was married to Ana Katarina Frankopan (d. 1673) with whom he had a son, Ivan Antun, and three daughters: Judita Petronila and Veronika who became nuns, and Jelena (1643–1693), who married first Franjo Rákóczy and later Emerik Tököly.  
Petar Zrinski along with other distinguished noblemen – his brother-in-law Franjo Krsto Frankopan, Franjo Nadasdy and Erasmus Tattenbach – were accused and tried for conspiracy against the Absolutist rule of Emperor Leopold I Habsburg. Found guilty, execution of the conspirators took place at Wiener Neustadt on 30 April 1671. On the eve of his death, Petar wrote a famous goodbye letter in Croatian to his wife Katarina, beginning with the words “My dear heart …” After his death the huge Zrinski estates in Croatia were confiscated and plundered.  
The portrait shows Petar Zrinski dressed as a wealthy nobleman, with the Zrinski coat of arms in the upper left-hand corner. Painted for the monastery in Svetice near Karlovac, Croatia, this portrait together with the portrait of Emperor Leopold I, are by an unknown Pauline artist. Pairing up the two portraits – *Petar Zrinski* and *Emperor Leopold I* – suggests that both were produced before the conspiracy and trial, some time before 1670.
d1d8cb50-1251-5dab-a6ce-97b1c120592b.short_description: A portrait of the Croat nobleman, Count Petar Zrinski, who excelled in battles against the Turks and was executed for treason by Emperor Leopold I.

Eidémq(ue) forum Ecclesiae / Vicinum imperpetuat 1646*”, indicating that the painting was for the Pauline monastery in Svetice, Croatia. Further confirmation of the date and origin of the work relies on documentation in the Museum inventory.

d367a154-49f9-5be0-a44e-c1259f9e26e2.name: *Anna Maria Victoria Jabornigg-Gamseneck*
d367a154-49f9-5be0-a44e-c1259f9e26e2.description:
A portrait of a finely dressed and learned noblewoman in an ermine pelisse, she sits on a chair by a table on which are geometrical implements, several books and some sheets of paper.  
The painting is thought to be a portrait of Maria Victoria Jabornigg Gamsenegg, the first wife of Josip Ignac Sigismund Hilleprand-Prandau, son of Petar II Anton.  
Attributed to Ephraim Hochhauser who studied at the Vienna Academy and made his name painting portraits of the aristocracy, perhaps the identity of the sitter in this case is less important than the context. The woman holding compasses in her hand sits in front of sheets of drawing paper, a ruler and protractor. At the time, geometry was an acceptable form of entertainment for amateurs and seen as part of a good education. With a little freedom of thought, we might link these items with the laying out of the Baroque *parterre* garden in front of Valpovo Manor.  
The History Gallery of the Hungarian National Museum in Budapest has an identical portrait, which according to researchers represents Maria Christina the beloved daughter of Empress Maria Theresia, and attributed to the court painter Martin van Meytens who was a great favourite of the Empress. Since Petar II Hilleprand-Prandau was in the diplomatic service of the Austrian Court, it is possible that a portrait of the Empress's daughter found its way to Valpovo Manor.
d367a154-49f9-5be0-a44e-c1259f9e26e2.short_description:
A portrait of a finely dressed and learned noblewoman, which according to the Prandau family archive, is a portrait of Anna Maria Victoria – the first wife of Josip Ignac – son of Petar II Anton.  
There is an identical portrait in the History Gallery of the Hungarian National Museum by Martin van Meytens, which according to researchers shows Maria Christina, daughter of Empress Maria Theresia.  
Perhaps the identity of the sitter in this case is less important than the context, for the woman holding compasses in her hand sits amidst sheets of drawing paper, a ruler and protractor. At the time, geometry was an acceptable form of entertainment for amateurs and seen as part of a good education. With a little freedom of thought, we might link these items with the laying out of the Baroque *parterre* garden in front of Valpovo Manor.

d435d9f4-9833-55f4-b40f-d413ab1c10be.name: *Portrait of Domenico Scarlatti*
d435d9f4-9833-55f4-b40f-d413ab1c10be.description:
Court Maestro to the exiled Polish queen Maria Kazimiera, and responsible for the Vatican's *Capella Giulia*, Domenico Scarlatti (1685–1757) was hired in 1714 as *Kappelmeister* by the Marquis of Fontes, Ambassador to King D. João V, at the Court of Pope Clement XI.  
Scarlatti's arrival in Portugal was a result of the high praise he had received from the King of Portugal's brother, Prince D. António who had attended one of his concerts in Rome. Scarlatti arrived in Portugal in around 1720 to become Princess Maria Barbara and Prince D. Jose's music teacher. Meanwhile the Pope had consented to the upgrade of the Royal Chapel to a Patriarchal Chapel and Scarlatti was invited to become *Kappelmeister* of the orchestra and choir of the Patriarchal Seminar Chapel.  
The Neapolitan Scarlatti's contribution to the Portuguese music scene was immense, he introduced Italian Opera, and the new musical and artistic patterns in vogue all over Europe at the time.  
In 1729 Scarlatti moved to Madrid to become once again Princess Maria Bárbara's music master, who by this time had married the Prince of Asturias, son of King Philip V and future King Philip VI of Spain. He remained in Spain until his death in 1757.  
Under the patronage of King D. João V, Domenico Scarlatti lived with his family in Spain where he enjoyed all the preconditions necessary to enhance his musical career and ensure his notoriety grew among his European musical peers.  
The art of portraiture peaked in the 18th century, fuelled by commissions from the European monarchs. Artists such as Louis Michel Van Loo, court painter to King Philip V of Spain (grandson of Louis XIV) between 1738 and 1752, or Jean Ranc (1674–1735) gained notoriety. The latter also painted the Portuguese Royal family following H. Rigaud.  
So it was that the Spanish artist Domingos António Velasco painted this portrait of Scarlatti in the Van Loo style in around 1739. Velasco depicts the maestro standing in front of an opulently painted curtain, his body twisted to the right and his hand resting on a wooden box. The light falls on the musician's face and hands, and he is dressed in a golden yellow and grey-blue ceremonial court vestment, adorned with the prestigious St James, a cognizance bestowed upon him one year previously by King D. João V, Grand-Master of the Order.

João V and the Queen of Spain, this portrait of Domenico Scarlatti is by the Spanish painter Domingos António Velasco. The artist depicts Scarlatti dressed in a ceremonial court vestment, adorned with the prestigious Order of St. James, a cognizance bestowed upon him one year previously by King D. João V, Grand-Master of the Order.

d4c7f9c0-dc66-5391-8685-09943014060f.name: Gjorche Petrov
d4c7f9c0-dc66-5391-8685-09943014060f.short_description: Gjorche Petrov (1865–1921) was a prominent member of the Internal Macedonian Revolutionary Organization (VMRO). He was born in Prilep on 2 March 1865. He obtained his elementary education in his native town and attended gymnasium in present day Bulgaria. He worked as a teacher in several Macedonian towns. He worked out, together with Gotze Delchev, the Statute of VMRO. The aim of the organization clearly expressed in Article 1 of the Statute was attaining full political autonomy of Macedonia and the Adrianopole Region. The structure of the organization was also defined as consisting of village, regional and district committees and lead by the Central Committee. Becoming one of the leaders of the Internal Macedonian Revolutionary Organization he shared Gotze Delchev’s conviction that the uprising was not supposed to begin before all regions in Macedonia were fully prepared for it in terms of training of the troops and providing arms.
d4c7f9c0-dc66-5391-8685-09943014060f.author: Nada Andonovska (author), Dragan Georgiev, historian (consultant)

d6484564-de31-5ad5-b6c7-ba70506e3e5f.name: *The Gourmet*
d6484564-de31-5ad5-b6c7-ba70506e3e5f.description:
Jacob van Schuppen studied painting with his father – Pierre Louis van Schuppen a painter and engraver in Antwerp – and his uncle, Nicolas Largillière, one of the period's most respected portrait painters. This beginning determined both his career and his preferred genre. Van Schuppen worked both in Paris and at the Lorraine princely court in Luneville as a portrait painter. In 1705, he became a member of the Paris Academy, arriving in Vienna in 1716 as a successful and notable portraitist in the service of Prince Eugene of Savoy. Having been settled in the imperial city for only a short time, he became court painter in 1723. In 1725, he approached the emperor with a plan for a French-style art academy, which he directed from 1726. Vienna's Imperial and Royal Court Academy of Painters, Sculptors and Architecture (Academy of Fine Arts Vienna) was unprecedented in Central Europe and remained the most important institution of its kind in the German-speaking territories. As a painter, van Schuppen was primarily an excellent portraitist. His large-size portraits, representing the aristocracy and contemporary writers and artists, effectively reflect the personality and character of the sitters.  
*The Gourmet*, although for a long time registered as a work of a German master, is an excellent example of van Schuppen's art, holding the characteristic features of his work. Like his other paintings, the motifs of both genre painting and still life are present.  
The objective approach of Dutch and Flemish art, fine colouring and French elegance come together in this painting; the basic motif – a man uplifting his glass to demonstrate his aspirations in seeking happiness in drinking and smoking: the minor pleasures of life – is a favourite and frequent characteristic of 17th-century painters. Although known primarily as a portraitist, van Schuppen nevertheless approached genre painting in a similar way, as can be seen in this painting and others in Hungarian collections.
d6484564-de31-5ad5-b6c7-ba70506e3e5f.short_description: Jacob van Schuppen, from the Netherlands, was a pupil of his uncle Nicolas Largilliere. From 1716 he lived in Vienna, and from 1726 directed the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna, breathing new life into the institution, which was renamed the Imperial and Royal Court Academy of Painters, Sculptors and Architecture. *The Gourmet*, showing a man enjoying the finer things of life, is both a portrait and a genre painting.
d6484564-de31-5ad5-b6c7-ba70506e3e5f.obtention: Initially from the Esterházy Collection in Pottendorf, in 1867 Endre Pánthy acquired the painting. From 1906, it was in the Lyceum school’s substantial collection in Eger as part of the Endre Pánthy legacy. It was then transferred to the Dobó István Castle Museum in Eger.

d6720426-2881-5b4a-8e11-89649a430aa6.name: *Loie Fuller: the serpentine dance*
d6720426-2881-5b4a-8e11-89649a430aa6.short_description: Mary Louise Fuller was an American dancer who lived in Europe for many years. As an artist, she was inspired by her travels and by new inventions - the dance of the veils (the "serpentine" dance) mixes Arab influences with light tricks using electricity. Loie Fuller was an important influence in the Art Nouveau and Symbolist movements, and helped train other great artists such as Isadora Duncan. The "serpentine dance" was imitated by many artists, and inspired the first cinematographers, such as the Lumière brothers, who dedicated a short film to it.
keywords: Dance; Orientalism; electricity

d6bf4415-f421-5f22-a960-431f5321ca7c.name: Shah Jahan and Dara Shikoh
d6bf4415-f421-5f22-a960-431f5321ca7c.short_description: Dara Shikoh was the favourite son and designated heir of the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan (r. 1627–58). However, Dara never acceded to the throne, for in 1659 he was killed during the war of succession that ensued when his father fell ill in 1657. Both men are heavily bejewelled, wearing mainly pearls, emeralds and rubies. Shah Jahan, with a partially greyed beard and wearing a fur-collared jacket, offers a large ruby (or spinel) to Dara. The European-style angels hovering above symbolize imperial majesty, while the globe on which father and son stand more precisely denotes Shah Jahan’s perceived status as King of the World (which is the English translation of the title ‘Shah Jahan’).
keywords: portrait; portraiture; jewel; jewellery; symbolism; allegory; textile; royal; border decoration; arabesque; miniature painting; floral decoration; angel; arms
materials: Coloured pigments and gold on paper

d6e29c37-877d-59fc-ba89-0136adddb6e7.name: Wedding portrait of King Aleksandar and Queen Draga of Serbia
d6e29c37-877d-59fc-ba89-0136adddb6e7.description: At the end of the 19th and during the first decade of the 20th century Pirot kilims served as unavoidable decor in public buildings and in important public manifestations. An official wedding photo of King Alexander Obrenović of Serbia and Queen Draga, shows a royal couple standing on the Pirot kilims, used as floor coverings in this solemn occasion as distinguished national products. The official photograph, taken on 4 August 1900 by the court photographer Milan Jovanović, was issued on a poster by the bookstore of Sreten J. Djordjević and printed by the State Printing House of the Kingdom of Serbia.

He focused on Ottoman clothing and street vendors in 1860.

d86bffa6-0320-50d5-b0a4-c47134d7d642.name: Water pumping equipment in Kağıthane, Istanbul
d86bffa6-0320-50d5-b0a4-c47134d7d642.short_description: During the 19th century, new technologies radically transformed both travel and communications. Cendere Hamidian Water Pump Station was built by Abdülhamid II in 1902 at an altitude of 34 metres above sea level. With its function, architectural design and mechanical equipment, the station is a unique monument to the history of the architecture industry in the Ottoman Empire. It pumped to Balmumcu and Beşiktaş – in the direction of Tophane, moving water coming from 20 different pipes in Kağıthane using steam pump machines.

d9278f88-7c6f-5ba2-a99d-94b0d6496626.short_description: With the political developments of the 19th century, interest in the East increased steadily in the western world. Everything belonging to the East was the centre of interest for western observers. As a result, close to 160 artists visited Istanbul in the 19th century. Born in Costantinople in 1851, Nicolas Andriomenos was an Ottoman Greek who learned photography in the 1870s from Cosmi Abdullah. At that time, Cosmi operated a studio of his own in Beyazıt, but turned the business over to Andriomenos in late 1879, after which its new proprietor soon made it into one of the city's most prestigious portrait studios.

d9708463-f720-5673-ac88-cf01adf12b47.name: *Portrait of a Greek Wearing a Fustanela*
d9708463-f720-5673-ac88-cf01adf12b47.short_description: It may depict a notable of Aighion, Andreas Londos (1786–1846) who entertained Lord Byron on his first visit to Greece. The picture is similar in style, setting and pose to that entitled ‘Un Grec de Janina’ in Dupré’s *Voyage à Athènes et Constantinople*, 1825. Louis Dupré (1798–1837) was one of the most talented painters who travelled to Greece. He arrived in 1819. The French artist who was an ardent philhellene published in 1825 a set of coloured lithographs of views and studies of costumes from Greece, entitled *Voyage a Athènes et Constantinople*.
d9708463-f720-5673-ac88-cf01adf12b47.author: Tsigakou 1984, 195
keywords: travels; Greece; Dupre

da83b646-c418-524e-8eff-75e69c1f77d9.name: Danilo I, Prince of Montenegro (1871–1939) and Princess Jutta of Mecklenburg-Strelitz
da83b646-c418-524e-8eff-75e69c1f77d9.short_description: Danilo I, Prince of Montenegro (1871–1939) with his wife, Princess Jutta von Mecklenburg-Strelitz. Danilo was the eldest son of King Nicola I of Montenegro. He was married to Princess Jutta von Mecklenburg-Strelitz and had to leave Montenegro after it was integrated in the kingdom of Yugoslavia after WWI. He died in 1937 in Vienna, Austria – in exile.
keywords: Danilo I, Prince of Montenegro; Jugoslavia; Vienna; Austria

dcf06086-9092-5d9d-bf04-d94e167662b6.name: Turkish women
dcf06086-9092-5d9d-bf04-d94e167662b6.short_description: The Zangaki brothers were a pair of photographers working in Egypt who sold "Orientalist" photos to Western toursits, allowing them to immortalise their trip to the "Orient". This photograph shows two Turkish women, probably mother and daughter, in formal dress.

deb4b3a7-5e57-5235-b533-346c36e88be2.name: *Mahmud II, Sultan of Turkey* (1784–1839)
deb4b3a7-5e57-5235-b533-346c36e88be2.short_description:
Portrait of Mahmud II, Sultan of Turkey (1784–1839). In 1826 Mahmud II initiated the development of a modern army. This led to the uprising of the Janissary, which was quelled by massacring the rebellious troops. Under Mahmud II's reign, in 1821 the Greeks started their fight for freedom which was granted to them in the Peace of Adrianople in 1829.  
After the destruction of the Janissary, the Ottoman Empire under Sultan Mahmud II had only 35,000 badly trained regular soldiers in 1827. Due to the weakness of the Ottoman Empire, Ibrahim Pasha, the son of Muhammad 'Ali (ruler of Egypt), invaded Syria. On 20 February 1832, the Egyptian Army defeated the Ottoman Army at the Battle of Konya. This forced Mahmud II to sign the Peace of Kütahya and to cede Syria and Kilikia to Egypt.
keywords: Mahmud II, Sultan of Turkey; Egypt; Janissary; Konya; Ibrahim Pasha; Muhammad Ali; Greece

dfe6e123-1970-5707-8279-08002d40fd1f.name: Ottoman Clothing Album
dfe6e123-1970-5707-8279-08002d40fd1f.short_description: With the political developments of the 19th century, interest in the East increased steadily in the western world. Everything belonging to the East was the centre of interest for western observers. As a result, close to 160 artists visited Istanbul in the 19th century. Pascal Sébah (1823-86) was a pioneer photographer who worked in Istanbul. Sébah opened a photography studio known as "El Chark " in Pera in 1857. The studio's most successful period started with the Vienna Universal Exhibition in 1873. Sébah formed a partnership with Joaillier Polycarpe in 1885. In 1899, the two partners bought Abdullah Frères's archives. For the Vienna Universal Exhibition in 1873, Pascal Sébah prepared *The Ottoman Clothing Album* to be exhibited at the Ottoman Stand.
dfe6e123-1970-5707-8279-08002d40fd1f.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)
dfe6e123-1970-5707-8279-08002d40fd1f.dates: Late 19th century – beginning of the 20th century
keywords: Yıldız Album; II. Abdulhamid Han; Photograph Ancient Istanbul; Pascal Sebah

e189b316-270d-52f6-bc71-843ad7287741.name: Bookcover
e189b316-270d-52f6-bc71-843ad7287741.short_description: A pair of Qajar lacquered binding depicts Fath ʽAli Shah (r. 1797–1834) on the front cover, in his famous majestic pose clad in elaborate jewelled regalia and wearing his grander imperial crown, the Taj-e Kiyani, commissioned upon his accession in 1798. The back cover depicts a court scene, landscape, court and decoration. The king shown here is Mohammad Shah Qajar (r. 1834–1848), son of Fath ‘Ali Shah. Few minor differences in number of people, their cloth design and the objects, can also be noticed. The inner cover is decorated in a reversed composition. The main panel is adorned with a central scalloped medallion, two small pendants above and below and corner-pieces containing red and yellow rose bushes on green ground. The parts of the central field between the centre and corner-pieces are filled with gold painted flower and leaf motifs. The panel is framed with three borders; the middle border has a red ground with red and yellow rose bushes arranged between two borders with gold flower and leaf motifs on black ground. Although the patron of the cover has not been identified, the painting suggests that it could be the cover of a *muraqqa’* (album) or royal documents which was either commissioned by the Shah himself or by a prince or wealthy court official. In addition, although the binding is unsigned and undated, the quality of workmanship suggests that it was painted by one of the fine painters in the court ateliers. The spine has been removed and the gap has been closed.

e396b7b2-cb07-51d7-86f1-b131b11dbfe2.name: Portrait of a lady of the court playing the tambourine
e396b7b2-cb07-51d7-86f1-b131b11dbfe2.short_description: This painting is one of the four half-length portraits painted by Pierre Désiré Guillemet in 1874-1875 depicting a young woman of the Ottoman Court. Her dress has been emphasized by means of a neutral background. She is wearing a *dört etek* (four-skirted) robe, made of *savai* fabric. Part of her undershirt with embroidered borders is visible from her large sleeves and around the edges of the robe. Her robe has a floral pattern with lively colours and her belt has a clasp with a two large stones in a silver setting. Her chestnut-coloured hair flows down to her shoulder. She wears two strands of pearls around her neck and a gold earing with pearls and gems. On her head she wears a cap of blue fabric decorated with small white flowers, plumes and toile.
keywords: Pierre Desire Guillemet; Orientalism; painting; İstanbul

e50ae40d-d2e5-50ff-9f8d-f861d8f298d4.name: *Woman from Constantine*
e50ae40d-d2e5-50ff-9f8d-f861d8f298d4.short_description: This painting belonged first to the collection at St. Martin's Church, Cologne, then to the Duchess of Reggio. It can be found in the catalogue written by the art historian Léonce Bénédite on Chassériau (see vol. 2, p. 495; cf. André Dezarrois, *Théodore Chassériau, sa Vie et son Œuvre*). The artist used women from the Jewish community in Constantine as models for woman's face and dress, following Dehodencq's example from his time in Morocco. This explains her resemblance to Rachel's portrait, which is also kept in the museum.
e50ae40d-d2e5-50ff-9f8d-f861d8f298d4.author: Dalila Orfali

e532dd30-df15-5462-88cf-6f2eaa8cf7bd.name: Portrait of David Roberts, Esq., R. A.
e532dd30-df15-5462-88cf-6f2eaa8cf7bd.short_description: This engraving shows a portrait of David Roberts (1796 – 1864), first completed in the 1840s by Charles Baugniet. Roberts is shown seated on an ancient plinth or capital, holding a drawing board and a pencil. A classical temple structure appears in the background on the left. David Roberts was a Scottish painter especially known for a prolific series of detailed lithograph prints of Egypt and the Near East produced during the 1840s from sketches he made during extensive tours of the region (1838–1839). These, and his large oil paintings of similar subjects, made him a prominent and highly influential Orientalist painter. Charles-Louis Baugniet (1814 - 1886), was a Belgian artist famous for the lithographing of portraits of prominent European figures.
e532dd30-df15-5462-88cf-6f2eaa8cf7bd.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Department

e5c4e1fa-cda0-5a71-9b74-c7a6f465f4ad.short_description: This oil on canvas is a portrait of Hammouda Pacha Bey before the dress code reform, in traditional dress with a cashmere shawl and dagger in his right hand. Hammouda Pacha Bey, nicknamed the builder of modern Tunisia, was a qualified and military man and was known as a firm but fair ruler.

e608c729-04c2-56e1-b2e3-0064a245a0ed.name: *Portrait of Historian, Márton György Kovachich*
e608c729-04c2-56e1-b2e3-0064a245a0ed.description:
Messerschmidt was born in south-west Germany. After studying in Munich and Graz, he matriculated at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna in 1755. Having graduated, he was employed at the Imperial Arms collection. During the period 1760–69 his work followed the artistic style of the Late Baroque court, at that time under the determining influence of Balthasar Ferdinand Moll. From 1769, Messerschmidt's first Neo-Classical works appear and to which he applied the experiences of his study trip to Rome in 1765. In 1770–72, Messerschmidt began to work on his so-called *Character Heads*, obviously connected with certain paranoid ideas and hallucinations from which, at the beginning of the 1770s, the master began to suffer. After an unsuccessful application to the office of a leading professor at the Academy, in 1777, he settled down in Pozsony (Bratislava) where he dedicated himself primarily to his *Character Heads* and in addition made other portraits as well.  
The bust of Márton György Kovachich (1743–1821), a historian, a custodian of the Buda university library, and one of the most eminent scholars of the Enlightenment in Hungary, was the last of these commissions in Messerschmidt's oeuvre. Kovachich commissioned the portrait directly from the artist in Pozsony (Bratislava), a fact corroborated by a letter from Kovachich dated 1 May 1783, at which time the portrait was already standing in his room in Buda. Like the *Character Heads* the bust is made in the early Neo-Classical style preferred by Messerschmidt since 1769–70. His works of this period have an accentuated plainness, but nevertheless have a vigorous modelling and structure. The portraits have a timeless, monumental character enhanced by their firm portraiture, one marked by the face-on portrayal of his subject. These stylistic characteristics of the Neo-Classical aesthetic are, however, coupled with an exact portrayal of the sitter's features, so that Messerschmidt's portraits remain very close to a realistic appraisal of human individuality.
e608c729-04c2-56e1-b2e3-0064a245a0ed.short_description: Messerschmidt moved to Vienna and later to Pozsony (Bratislava) from Bavaria. He made his famous *Character Heads* in Pozsony (Bratislava) when he was mentally ill. All of them portray the features of the artist. The bust of the historian, Kovachich, was made by the artist at a time when he his mental health was good.

e7547eb9-bf91-59b1-a040-daa53056b7e6.name: *Maria Eleonora Regina Johanna Juliana Pejačević* born *Erdödy de Monyorokerek*
e7547eb9-bf91-59b1-a040-daa53056b7e6.description:
Countess Eleonora, depicted in a garden offering incense into an urn that stands in front of a statue of Cupid, has just married Count Karlo III Pejačević who is 25 years her senior; she is his second wife. Her dress is of fine, expensive material decorated with pearls. Her grey, powdered hair is also dressed with pearls.  
Marija Eleonora was born into the Erdödy family, members of which played a very important role in the history of Croatia.  
The Pejačević family, originally from Bulgaria, was one of the aristocratic families to whom the Habsburg Crown granted land in Slavonia after its liberation from the Ottomans.  
The painter of this portrait, J. G. Weickert, belonged to the generation of Austrian Rococo painters, the work of which already demonstrated components of the Neo-Classical style, which is especially visible in this portrait. For example, the pastel colours and charming grace of the countess' slender and vivacious figure, still in the Rococo style, have been infiltrated by undefined changes of tone, a degree of measure and a breath of melancholy underlined by the ambient Neo-Classical architecture.  
This is more than the portrait of a person: the content of the painting shows the countess herself in a symbolic act of throwing incense into an urn in front of a statuette of Cupid, an act supplicating happiness in marriage. Considering that the countess was 19 years old and that she had just married a man 25 years her senior, there were definite reasons to eternalise this act.  
In style, the portrait heralds the new age of the Enlightenment.
e7547eb9-bf91-59b1-a040-daa53056b7e6.short_description: A portrait of Countess Maria Eleonora Pejačević, who by birth and marriage, belonged to two important noble families in Croatia. The painting is by the Austrian painter, J. G. Weickert, who was working during the Rococo period but whose paintings already show influences of the Neo-classical style. In this painting, the Neo-classical style is especially apparent, while it also announces the new spirit of the Enlightenment.

e7be577c-7197-59de-94eb-bd3d5d7cdba0.name: Portrait of emperor Shah Jahan, his three sons, and Asaf Khan
e7be577c-7197-59de-94eb-bd3d5d7cdba0.short_description: In this royal family portrait, Emperor Shah Jahan (r. 1628–58), sitting in haloed profile upon a gold-footed throne under a high white canopy, accepts a jewelled gift from his father-in-law, Asaf Khan. At his right are his three eldest sons—Dara Shikoh (1615–59), Shah Shija (1616–59), and the ill-fated Awrangzeb (r. 1618–1707), whose death effectively marked the end of the great Mughal Empire. All figures are resplendent in turbans decorated with jewels, pearl necklaces, different types of daggers (*khilanum*, *katar*, and *kard*), lavishly embroidered sashes, and gilded swords. An illuminated carpet lies underfoot.

e80567bb-4a41-5dd5-a8c2-8530ecf7b427.name: Abdelaziz Thâalbi (Abdelaziz al-Thalibi)
e80567bb-4a41-5dd5-a8c2-8530ecf7b427.short_description: Born in Tunis in 1876, Abdelaziz Thâalbi (Abdelaziz al-Thalibi) was a Tunisian politician. In 1920, he became the founder of the political party Destour, and participated in all the first fights of the nationalist movement. This activism caused him to be sent into exile in 1912, not for the first time, with six other nationalist politicians. In 1920 he wrote and published the manifesto La Tunisie Martyre with Ahmed Sakka, for which he was arrested on 31 July and taken to Tunis. However, feeling threatened there, he fled and left Tunisia once again in 1923. Destourian militants in Tunisia kept calling for his return, which finally happened in July 1937, 14 years after being forced into exile. However, upon his return he entered into conflict with Neo-Destour politicians, led by Bourguiba. He died on 1 October 1944, and his funeral was an opportunity for the Neo-Destour movement, as well as all the fringes of the nationalist movement to gather, and pay tribute to one of the founding fathers of Tunisian nationalism

e80567bb-4a41-5dd5-a8c2-8530ecf7b427.author: Bechir Yazidi
keywords: The Young Tunisians movement; "La Tunisie Martyre"

e87a28c8-480d-590e-ba3c-b84ef6e8d476.name: Abdul-Mejid I, Sultan of Turkey (1823–1861)
e87a28c8-480d-590e-ba3c-b84ef6e8d476.short_description: Portrait of Abdul-Mejid I, Sultan of Turkey (1823–1861), riding a horse. When he came to power in 1839, he tried to re-occupy lands lost to Muhammad 'Ali Pasha, the ruler of Egypt. In this effort he was supported by Britain and Austria. In 1840 a combined British-Austrian fleet cut off the supply lines of the Egyptian army and forced the Egyptians to sign the 1840 Convention of Alexandria. Abdul-Mejid was able to win back Syria and Palestine. In 1849 he granted the Hungarian refugees exile. In 1861 he died and left his throne to his brother Abdülaziz.
keywords: Abdul-Mejid, Sultan of Turkey; Egypt; Syria, Palestine; Hungarian refugees

ea69f41d-1b91-5ee4-8097-8aba9db33c0f.name: *Le consul Joseph Raffo* (painting)
ea69f41d-1b91-5ee4-8097-8aba9db33c0f.short_description: Giuseppe Maria Joseph Raffo, the subject of this painting, was born in Tunis in 1795 and is depicted here in full uniform with the air of an important Turkish dignitary. He entered service as a secretary to Bey Hassine, and later served as Tunisia's Minister for Foreign Affairs under his rule as well as that of his successors, despite being a Sardinian subject all the while. He made a fortune by taking over a tuna farm in the Cap Bon region in the form of private concession. This painting is evidence of an active diplomatic relationship between the Palais du Bardo and the European chancelleries.

ed505641-7fab-598f-a27b-c58fb38cc49e.name: Portrait of the Ottoman Sultan Ahmed I.
ed505641-7fab-598f-a27b-c58fb38cc49e.description:
This miniature painting executed in gouache on paper is a portrait of the Ottoman Sultan Ahmed I (AH 1012–26 / AD 1603–17) and once formed part of an album that contained both Ottoman Turkish and Persian miniatures, apparently assembled in the AH 12th / AD 18th century. The youthful ruler, best known as the founder of the Blue Mosque in Istanbul, is seated on a large, richly decorated throne beneath a cusped arch. He is leaning against a decorated bolster wearing a white turban enhanced by two tall plumes issuing from bejewelled sockets. His green and gold-brocade caftan has large, gold globular buttons down the front. The garment is secured by a jewel-studded gold belt, which incorporates three cusped, circular units at the front. A bejeweled dagger handle can be seen protruding from Sultan Ahmed’s belt on the right. He wears a red-orange overcoat with small gold buttons down the front; the coat is lined with ermine. A gold-coloured slipper protrudes from underneath his garments. In his left hand, the fifth finger of which is enhanced by a gold ring with circular stone, Sultan Ahmed holds the *mandil*, a ceremonial handkerchief with gold detailing. In his right hand he holds a volume of poetry bound in the so-called *sefine* format (with the vertically oriented pages bound at the top, narrow end). The gilt binding shows a delicately drawn, central medallion enclosed within an elongated, arched cartouche.  
Above the portrait of the sultan runs a cursive inscription contained within two elongated cusped cartouches, written in white against a blue background and enhanced by white floral detailing, it reads: ‘Hasrat Sultan Ahmad \[Ahmed\] ibn Sultan Muhammad \[Mehmed\] Khan’. A tiny inscription on the lower left-hand side of the work names the painter ‘al-fakir Süleyman’. The portrait is surrounded by a green inner frame and an orange outer frame with additional ruled frames in blue, red, gold and green in between and around the outside of the outer border.
ed505641-7fab-598f-a27b-c58fb38cc49e.short_description: This miniature painting shows the Ottoman Sultan Ahmed I, best known as the founder of the Blue Mosque in Istanbul. It has been suggested that this portrait was executed in the court workshops of the Topkapı Saray in Istanbul during the early AH 11th / AD 17th century.

ed505641-7fab-598f-a27b-c58fb38cc49e.method_for_datation: It is assumed that this portrait was painted during or just after the lifetime of Sultan Ahmed I (r. 1012–26 / 1603–17).
ed505641-7fab-598f-a27b-c58fb38cc49e.method_for_provenance: It has been suggested that this portrait was executed in the Court workshops of the Topkapı Saray in Istanbul during the early 11th / early 17th century.

ee0cbe27-f7a7-56db-b5c5-18038a38b0c8.name: Omar Pasha (1806–1871)
ee0cbe27-f7a7-56db-b5c5-18038a38b0c8.short_description: Portrait of Omar Pasha. He was born in Croatia in 1806 near the Turkish-Hungarian border. In 1828 he deserted from the Austrian army and joined the Ottoman administration in Bosnia. After a long career in the Ottoman army, he became the military governor of Bucharest and commanded the Ottoman forces at the siege of Sevastopol in Crimea. In 1862 he suppressed an uprising in Herzogovina and led a victorious campaign against Montenegro. In 1868 he became War Minister and died in 1871 in Istanbul.

eefedc43-2cbd-5fa9-9062-25f5724872cf.name: *Self Portrait*
eefedc43-2cbd-5fa9-9062-25f5724872cf.description:
The portrait painter, Ádám Mányoki, was one of the most prominent figures of Baroque art in Hungary. His career began in Hanover and Hamburg and then, in the first decade of the 18th century, he worked for Frederick William at the Berlin court. From 1707 to 1712, he was court portraitist to Prince Ferenc Rákóczi II in Hungary, where he worked for a number of years before carrying out other assignments for the prince in the Netherlands and Berlin.  
He painted the *Self Portrait* rendered with a captivating candour and self-assurance in Berlin. He used a trick of the self-portraitist that had been popular since Rembrandt: the soft velvet hat with its upturned rim casting a warm, brown shadow over the upper half of his face. The painting reveals a synthesis of the influence of Antoine Pesne, a French portraitist of the Prussian court, and of Mányoki's studies in northern Germany. The choice of colours and some formal details are clearly traceable to Pesne's work, while some characteristic features of the composition are rooted in 17th-century Dutch and German painting, including Johann Heinrich Roos' self-portrait. Mányoki may have known Roos' self-portrait from an engraving by Philip Kilian and taken inspiration from it in the figure's posture and the shirt loosely opening in front.  
From 1713, Mányoki was employed by August II the Strong, King of Poland and Elector of Saxony; from 1717 he was portrait painter to the court. Thereafter he received an increasing number of commissions in Leipzig to portray the professors of the university, the well-to-do burghers and merchants and their families. In the mid-1720s, Mányoki, intent on repatriation, returned to Hungary for a short time. However, a lack of patronage and inability to make a living meant he left for Dresden again, this time for good. He adjusted his later work in the main to the expectations of 18th-century German middle-class art collectors.
eefedc43-2cbd-5fa9-9062-25f5724872cf.short_description:
The son of a Protestant clergyman in Szokolya, Mányoki studied art in Germany. Called back to Hungary by Prince Ferenc Rákóczi II in 1707, he remained there until 1712. Following the collapse of the struggle against the Habsburgs for independence led by the prince, he worked for the Polish-Saxon court in Dresden from 1713.  
Painted in Berlin, the *Self Portrait –* rendered with captivating candour and self-assurance –represents an excellent “French-style” example of the artist's portrait painting.

It was bought by the Association of Friends of the Art Museums, and from 1931 was on permanent deposit in museums with which the Friends were associated. From 1974 it has been in the Hungarian National Gallery.
